sources.title: Designmuseum Danmark — *Learning from Japan*
sources.supports: Strongest museum source for Japanese influence on Danish craft/design from ca. 1900 through the 20th century; materials, motifs, interiors, furniture, and tableware.

sources.title: Designmuseum Danmark — research/publications
sources.supports: Points to Mirjam Gelfer-Jørgensen’s research *Influences from Japan in Danish Art and Design 1870–2010*.

sources.title: SMK — *Japanomania in the North 1875–1918*
sources.supports: Museum account of Japonisme in Danish/Nordic art; useful for exchange without claiming direct continuity to today’s label.

sources.title: SMK — *Japanomania in the Nordic Countries* publication
sources.supports: Scholarly catalogue framing Nordic adoption of Japanese motifs and visual systems across decorative arts.

sources.title: Embassy of Japan in Denmark (2026) — Anne-Louise Sommer decoration
sources.supports: Official confirmation of long-running Danish museum work on Japanese art/design and mutual cultural understanding.

sources.title: Japan Folk Crafts Museum — history
sources.supports: First-party history of Sōetsu Yanagi, the 1925 coining of *mingei*, the 1936 museum, ordinary craft, and the designed museum interior.

sources.title: Japan Folk Crafts Museum — Sōetsu Yanagi and the Mingeikan
sources.supports: Detailed Japanese-language institutional chronology: Korea, folk craft, Buddhism, exhibitions, model interiors, and museum formation.

sources.title: The Met — “The Japanese Tea Ceremony”
sources.supports: Museum scholarship showing eclectic tea-room objects and the historical development of rustic taste—far richer than “imperfection décor.”

sources.title: The Met — Shōin Room
sources.supports: Object/room source for tatami proportion, tokonoma, fusuma, craft technique, and Momoyama interior architecture.

sources.title: The Met — Kyoto exhibition guide
sources.supports: Tea-gathering room, decorative arts, lacquer, screens, ritual, and Kyoto’s multiple—not solely minimal—interior traditions.

sources.title: Japan House London — “Wabi-sabi and Japanese craft: nature or nurture?”
sources.supports: Japan specialist/craft framing for wabi-sabi; use to prevent a generic “distressed beige” translation.

sources.title: Designmuseum Danmark — *Danish Modern*
sources.supports: Authoritative Danish design history from the 1920s–2000, including Klint, Wegner, Juhl, Ditzel, Panton, and breaks with modernism.

sources.title: Aalto University — Alvar Aalto
sources.supports: University source on Aalto’s humanistic/natural modernism, total design, Artek, bent wood, and Aino/Elissa Aalto collaboration.

sources.title: Design Museum Helsinki — collections
sources.supports: Finnish design collection scope: objects, drawings, images, designer records, Arabia, Iittala, Nuutajärvi, and Hackman archives.

sources.title: Design Museum Helsinki — *Utopia Now: The Story of Finnish Design*
sources.supports: Museum narrative and digitized archive for Finnish design history; useful against treating “Scandi” as only Danish furniture.

sources.title: IKEA Museum — IKEA PS and Democratic Design
sources.supports: Manufacturer-museum source on 1990s revival/marketing of Scandinavian style and “Democratic Design.” Best used with the critical tier.

sources.title: Sompo Museum of Art — *Denmark Design*
sources.supports: Japanese museum view of Danish design from the late 19th century through mid-century and present; useful reception evidence.

sources.title: Japan Foundation — exhibition catalogue index, 1972–2022
sources.supports: First-party index to traveling exhibitions on Japanese design and craft, including *WA: The Spirit of Harmony and Japanese Design Today*.

sources.title: ADI Design Museum — *Origin of Simplicity: 20 Visions of Japanese Design*
sources.supports: Museum treatment of *ma*, *ku*, *wabi*, *sabi*, asymmetry, use, philosophy, and Italian/Japanese exchange; resists a one-note minimalism.

sources.title: Architectural Digest (2023) — “Japandi Style: Everything You Need to Know”
sources.supports: Clear record of mainstream 2020s usage, its component claims, and the term’s media consolidation. Treat its long-history assertions cautiously.

sources.title: Vogue (2025) — “What Is Japandi Style?”
sources.supports: High-visibility contemporary definition and practitioner quotes; useful evidence of the label’s market/social reach.

sources.title: Wallpaper* (2026) — modern Japanese houses
sources.supports: Current Japanese projects with architects’ own material/spatial explanations; useful to show Japanese design beyond a hybrid trend.

sources.title: Karimoku Case — Kinuta Terrace
sources.supports: First-party Japanese manufacturer case: Keiji Ashizawa + Norm Architects, 12 project-born pieces, courtyard/nature, durability, and material composition.

sources.title: Norm Architects — Kinuta Terrace
sources.supports: Danish practitioner’s account of a genuinely collaborative Tokyo renovation and furniture series—stronger evidence than a moodboard label.

sources.title: Keiji Ashizawa Design — Karimoku Case
sources.supports: Japanese practitioner’s account of the same collaboration, product development, real project needs, universality, and ongoing work.

sources.title: Wallpaper* (2026) — Japanese design at Milan Design Week
sources.supports: Current breadth: paper research, ceramics, lacquer/resin, reused timber, manufacturing, joinery, color, and play—not simply quiet beige.

sources.title: Wallpaper* (2026) — “Japanese design is interpreted through a Danish lens”
sources.supports: Best direct critique of “Japandi” as a marketable catch-all; stresses pragmatism, exacting craft, local manufacture, and relationships over moodboard similarity.

sources.title: UAL Research Online — “Yanagi Sōetsu and Korean crafts within the Mingei movement”
sources.supports: Postcolonial critique of Yanagi’s work in colonial Korea; prevents an uncritical “pure folk beauty” narrative.

sources.title: UC eScholarship — “Reimagining Decolonization in the Mingeikan”
sources.supports: Museum/decolonization research connecting the Mingeikan’s formation to memories and material legacies of Japanese colonialism in Korea.

sources.title: RISD Contemporary Aesthetics — “On Japanese Minimalism”
sources.supports: Academic challenge to the loose application of *ma*, *wabi-sabi*, and “Zen minimalism”; proposes more precise aesthetic vocabulary.

sources.title: Lund University — critical study of the Swedish modernist design project
sources.supports: Shows “Swedish/Scandinavian design” as a constructed, marketed unison rather than a neutral regional essence.

sources.title: Bloomsbury Academic — *Design by IKEA: A Cultural History*
sources.supports: Archive/interview-based critique of how IKEA promoted and profited from Swedishness, “design for everyone,” and Scandinavian Design.

sources.title: Design and Culture — “The Total Absence of Foreign Subjects”
sources.supports: Peer-reviewed analysis of racial politics in US exhibitions of Scandinavian design and the later reframing of “democratic” and “traditional.”
